UserGuide.generic.headerText: The page title confirms where you are and the main task you can complete here.
UserGuide.generic.workspaceText: Choose a scope or item first, then inspect the details. Forms, lists, and tabs update to match your selection.

UserGuide.studentCourse.title: Course page
UserGuide.courses.title: My Courses
UserGuide.courses.step1.title: Choose a course from your course list
UserGuide.courses.step1.text: All courses currently available to you appear here. During the tour, a dashed safe-demo course is added so you can practice opening one without changing real data.
UserGuide.courses.step2.title: This is the tour's simulated course
UserGuide.courses.step2.text: The ticket shows the title and class time and place, and the barcode on the stub is your practice progress, just like a real course. The dashed border and Safe demo label mean nothing is saved.
UserGuide.courses.step3.title: Open the course to see machines and weekly content
UserGuide.courses.step3.text: Next opens this simulated course and continues the tour through its classroom machine, learning progress, and weekly tasks.
UserGuide.studentCourse.step1.title: This week shows what to do now
UserGuide.studentCourse.step1.text: See this week's topic, whether you've marked it done, and your teacher's reply. Open this week to see each check's result.
UserGuide.studentCourse.step2.title: The bar shows how many of this week's checks passed
UserGuide.studentCourse.step2.text: It moves after your teacher runs the checks; marking the week done only tells your teacher you're finished.
UserGuide.studentCourse.step3.title: Enter your classroom machine here
UserGuide.studentCourse.step3.text: In a real course, select the machine card to start and enter its terminal or console. The info button opens complete settings. The simulation never starts a machine.
UserGuide.studentCourse.step4.title: Weekly content is collected here
UserGuide.studentCourse.step4.text: Each row is one week and shows its date, check count, and completion state. Each week has one overall completion checkbox.
UserGuide.studentCourse.step5.title: Open a week to see feedback and its machine
UserGuide.studentCourse.step5.text: Next opens the simulated first week and demonstrates check feedback, the machine selected for that week, and course materials.
UserGuide.courseWeek.title: Weekly Course Content
UserGuide.courseWeek.step1.title: Confirm the course, week, and date in the header
UserGuide.courseWeek.step1.text: First make sure you are in the correct course and week. Use Back to Course to return to the complete list of weeks.
UserGuide.courseWeek.step2.title: Review the latest feedback for each check here
UserGuide.courseWeek.step2.text: You can see status, score, and comments shared by your teacher or AI. Opening this page only shows results; it does not run the check again.
UserGuide.courseWeek.step3.title: This is the machine selected for the week
UserGuide.courseWeek.step3.text: In a real course, open a published service URL or go to the machine and console for full status. The simulation never creates or starts a machine.
UserGuide.courseWeek.step4.title: Weekly materials are collected here
UserGuide.courseWeek.step4.text: A material opens in a new tab. The simulated file only demonstrates its location and downloads nothing.
UserGuide.studentHome.title: Home
UserGuide.studentHome.step1.title: Start with your ongoing courses
UserGuide.studentHome.step1.text: Courses appear here for their entire duration, not just on class day. Green means the class is currently in session; you can still click into other courses to use machines, check assignments, or practice after class.
UserGuide.studentHome.step2.title: Quick practice doesn't need manual review
UserGuide.studentHome.step2.text: When you need to quickly test a command or do some lightweight practice, choose a template and fill in a container name and password — the system approves it automatically and starts creating it.
UserGuide.studentHome.step3.title: After-class practice or independent research
UserGuide.studentHome.step3.text: When it's not time for class, you can pick up where you left off in your last course from here; independent research takes you to a resource request instead.
UserGuide.myRequests.title: My Requests
UserGuide.myRequests.step1.title: This is the actual resource request form
UserGuide.myRequests.step1.text: The guide has taken you directly into the form. Use it for a project or independent-research VM/container; classroom machines assigned by a teacher do not need another request.
UserGuide.myRequests.step2.title: Ask AI when you are unsure what to enter
UserGuide.myRequests.step2.text: Open the AI assistant at the bottom-right and describe your goal, such as “I need to host a Python website for two weeks.” It will ask for missing details, recommend a suitable size, and help fill this form. You can still edit everything before submitting.
UserGuide.myRequests.step3.title: Name the resource, then choose an OS
UserGuide.myRequests.step3.text: The name helps you identify it later. Choosing an image or environment template determines whether a VM or container is created and loads its recommended base specification.
UserGuide.myRequests.step4.title: Match the hardware to the workload
UserGuide.myRequests.step4.text: More CPU, memory, and disk use more quota. The recommended values suit most sites and exercises; choose a VM or GPU only when a GUI, Windows, or accelerated compute is needed.
UserGuide.myRequests.step5.title: Set when you actually need it
UserGuide.myRequests.step5.text: Use Immediate when starting now or schedule exact dates for a course or planned task. An end date lets the system reserve and release resources correctly.
UserGuide.myRequests.step6.title: Explain the purpose for the reviewer
UserGuide.myRequests.step6.text: Briefly state the project, course, or service and why it needs these specifications. The AI assistant can also draft an editable reason from your previous choices.
UserGuide.myRequests.step7.title: The summary updates as you fill the form
UserGuide.myRequests.step7.text: Before submitting, verify the type, name, operating system, hardware, and period. Every change is reflected in this summary card.
UserGuide.myRequests.step8.title: Submit only after everything looks right
UserGuide.myRequests.step8.text: After submitting, you return to My Requests to track review and provisioning. Only this button creates the request; the guide itself never submits data.
UserGuide.myResources.title: My Resources
UserGuide.myResources.step1.title: These numbers are your usage quota
UserGuide.myResources.step1.text: The number on the left is your current usage; the one on the right is your available limit. For example, "2 / 4 units" means you've used 2 and can have up to 4. When you're close to the limit, you'll need to release a resource first.
UserGuide.myResources.step2.title: Each card represents one machine
UserGuide.myResources.step2.text: The IP is the machine's connection address; the status in the top-right corner shows whether it's usable. Click the machine name to see its full details.
UserGuide.myResources.step3.title: Use this button to enter the machine
UserGuide.myResources.step3.text: When the machine shows "Running", you can click "Terminal" or "Console" to start working. The three-dot button next to it lets you power on, shut down, or restart.
UserGuide.firewall.title: Firewall
UserGuide.firewall.step1.title: Step 1: Point at a dot on the source machine's edge
UserGuide.firewall.step1.text: First decide which machine the connection starts from. Hover over the source machine and connection dots appear on all four sides. You can start dragging from any of them; the line automatically leaves from the side closest to the destination.
UserGuide.firewall.dragMove.title: Step 2: Hold the dot and keep dragging
UserGuide.firewall.dragMove.text: Press and hold the left mouse button on the dot. Keep holding it while moving the pointer toward the destination machine. The animation demonstrates the full movement.
UserGuide.firewall.dragTarget.title: Step 3: Release over a dot on the destination machine
UserGuide.firewall.dragTarget.text: Move the pointer onto the center of a dot on the destination machine's edge and then release. A successful drop opens the connection settings so you can choose an allowed port. If nothing opens, try again and align with the dot more precisely.
UserGuide.firewall.step2.title: Or complete it with Add Connection
UserGuide.firewall.step2.text: If dragging is inconvenient, click "Add Connection" and choose the source, destination, and allowed port. There's no need to add one without a clear requirement.
UserGuide.firewall.step3.title: Lines represent currently allowed connections
UserGuide.firewall.step3.text: Each box represents a VM, and the lines between boxes represent allowed traffic. Click a VM to view its rules; the number on a line is the open port.
UserGuide.firewall.step4.title: These buttons only change how you view it
UserGuide.firewall.step4.text: "Auto-arrange" tidies up positions; "Connection labels" shows or hides ports; "Map" toggles the thumbnail in the bottom-right corner. None of these modify any firewall rules.
UserGuide.domain.title: Domain Management
UserGuide.domain.step1.title: Set up Cloudflare the first time you use this
UserGuide.domain.step1.text: Click "Connection Settings" and enter your Account ID and API Token. "Test Connection" only verifies that the settings are valid — it does not modify DNS.
UserGuide.domain.step2.title: This shows whether the connection is working
UserGuide.domain.step2.text: "Connected" means the platform can manage DNS; the last verified time helps you judge whether the credentials are still valid. Domains can't be loaded while disconnected.
UserGuide.domain.step3.title: The Zones number is how many domains you can manage
UserGuide.domain.step3.text: For example, "Zones (3)" means there are 3 domains available in the account. Click a domain on the left first, and its DNS records will appear on the right.
UserGuide.domain.step4.title: Search or add DNS records here
UserGuide.domain.step4.text: Use the search box to find existing records; "Add Record" creates a mapping between a name and an IP/service. If you're unsure about the record type, don't modify a production domain directly.
UserGuide.aiApi.title: AI API
UserGuide.aiApi.step2.title: Three tabs plus the Request Key dialog
UserGuide.aiApi.step2.text: Use Request Key to apply. API Keys holds your approved keys, Request History tracks reviews, and My Usage shows what your keys consume. Next, we'll walk through each step.
UserGuide.aiApi.step3.title: “+ Request Key”: request a new API key
UserGuide.aiApi.step3.text: Clicking this button opens the request dialog, telling the reviewer "which project needs AI and for how long". You won't get a key immediately after submitting — you'll need to wait for approval.
UserGuide.aiApi.step4.title: The key name is just for your own reference
UserGuide.aiApi.step4.text: We recommend entering your course or project name, such as "Capstone Project Chatbot". It is not the API key itself, and you can change it later.
UserGuide.aiApi.step5.title: The purpose of your request is shown to the reviewer
UserGuide.aiApi.step5.text: Write at least 10 characters, clearly describing the course, project, and the feature you plan to integrate — this is far easier for the reviewer to understand than just writing "test".
UserGuide.aiApi.step6.title: The validity period determines how long the key can be used
UserGuide.aiApi.step6.text: Choose a few days for short-term assignments, or a longer period for long-term projects. Once it expires, the API key stops working, but your request record isn't deleted.
UserGuide.aiApi.step7.title: Submit only once all information is complete
UserGuide.aiApi.step7.text: After you submit, the dialog closes and Request History opens so you can follow the review. Once approved, your key appears under API Keys.
UserGuide.aiApi.step8.title: API Keys: get the connection info your program needs
UserGuide.aiApi.step8.text: A key only appears on this page after your request is approved. Your program typically needs two values: the Base URL and the API Key. Treat the API Key like a password — don't paste it into assignments or public repositories. You'll find the Base URL and sample code under "API Quick Start".
UserGuide.aiApi.step9.title: Each row is one issued key
UserGuide.aiApi.step9.text: The status shows whether the key works, along with when it was created and when it expires. Inactive keys are collapsed below the table. If you see “No keys yet”, no request has been approved yet.
UserGuide.aiApi.step10.title: The difference between show, copy, regenerate, and disable
UserGuide.aiApi.step10.text: Click an underlined key name to view and copy the full key in its details dialog. The ⋮ menu holds Rename, Regenerate, and Disable. Regenerate invalidates the old key and opens a dialog with the full new key. Disabling prevents new calls; key and usage records remain, and accepted calls may still finish.
UserGuide.aiApi.step11.title: Request Records: Check where the review stands
UserGuide.aiApi.step11.text: Every AI API request you've submitted is kept on this page. It only shows the request and its review outcome — it's not where you retrieve keys.
UserGuide.aiApi.step12.title: Status and notes tell you what to do next
UserGuide.aiApi.step12.text: “Pending review” means it hasn't been processed yet. Once “Approved”, go to API Keys to get it. If “Rejected”, read the review comment and adjust your request.
UserGuide.aiApi.step13.title: My Usage: See how much AI your program has actually used
UserGuide.aiApi.step13.text: This page shows usage trends and token consumption — it doesn't display or modify your API Key. If usage spikes suddenly, check whether your program is calling the API repeatedly by mistake.
UserGuide.aiApi.step14.title: First choose the date range to analyze
UserGuide.aiApi.step14.text: The 7, 30, and 90-day options only change the report range — they don't limit your key's validity period. The dates on the right show the actual start and end dates currently covered by the report.
UserGuide.aiApi.step15.title: Unified usage: both routes combined into one total
UserGuide.aiApi.step15.text: Total calls sums the AI model route and the AI system route. Input Tokens is the text sent to the model, Output Tokens is what it returned, and you can inspect usage per model further below.
UserGuide.aiApi.step16.title: Call details: audit every single call
UserGuide.aiApi.step16.text: Each row lists the time, call type, model, tokens, and success/failure status. Failed calls include the error message to help you debug.
UserGuide.myResources.request.title: Request a resource here when the list is empty
UserGuide.myResources.request.text: Resource Request opens the full application form. Fill it yourself or ask the AI assistant in the bottom-right to organize your needs and help complete it.
UserGuide.myResources.row.title: Read a machine's status at a glance
UserGuide.myResources.row.text: The name, system, runtime state, private IP, expiry, and node are shown in one row. If you have no resources, this is safe sample data and creates nothing.
UserGuide.myResources.console.title: Connect to the machine here
UserGuide.myResources.console.text: LXC opens a terminal and a VM opens a graphical console. The machine must be running. The guide never makes a real connection.
UserGuide.myResources.power.title: More actions contains power and management tools
UserGuide.myResources.power.text: Start, shut down, reboot, or reset the machine here. With permission, you can also convert it to a template or delete it; risky actions still require confirmation.
UserGuide.myResources.detail.title: Open the machine name to see every setting
UserGuide.myResources.detail.text: Next, the guide enters this machine's detail page. If the account has no resources, it opens a read-only simulated detail page.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.title: Machine details and settings
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step1.title: Six tabs organize every machine function
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step1.text: The guide will open Overview, Monitoring, Specifications, Snapshots, Audit Logs, and Advanced Settings in sequence.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step2.title: Overview: status and access information
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step2.text: Find power state, IP, usage, expiry, and SSH or service links here. This is normally the first place to check.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step3.title: Monitoring: live and historical usage
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step3.text: Review CPU, memory, disk, and network traffic, then change the time range to decide whether resources need adjustment.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step4.title: Specifications: CPU, memory, and disk
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step4.text: Use the controls to request a specification change. Regular users submit for review; administrators can apply changes directly.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step5.title: Snapshots: recoverable points in time
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step5.text: Create a snapshot before upgrades or experiments and restore it when needed. The guide never creates, restores, or deletes one.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step6.title: Audit logs: who changed what and when
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step6.text: Power, specification, and settings changes appear here for troubleshooting and accountability.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step7.title: Advanced Settings: complete machine management
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step7.text: Lifecycle, firewall, boot options, login credentials, and sharing are explained next.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step8.title: Lifecycle and expiry
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step8.text: Manage expiry, automatic shutdown, and pending schedules. These settings affect when the machine stops or is reclaimed.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step9.title: Per-machine firewall
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step9.text: Manage allowed inbound and outbound traffic. Check source, protocol, and port carefully before saving.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step10.title: Boot devices and order
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step10.text: Prioritize disk, network, and ISO boot devices, and mount or unmount installation media.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step11.title: Passwords and SSH keys
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step11.text: Reset credentials, update the platform key, or add a personal SSH public key. Sensitive values only appear when needed.
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step13.title: Sharing and ownership
UserGuide.resourceDetail.step13.text: Grant access or transfer ownership. Verify the recipient and whether you retain access before transferring.
UserGuide.firewall.endpoints.title: The form first asks what you want to do
UserGuide.firewall.endpoints.text: The guide has opened the real Add Connection dialog. Pick an intent first: let a machine reach the internet, expose a service, connect two machines, or write a rule yourself. Then choose the machine and allowed ports; the direction follows the intent.
UserGuide.firewall.dialogActions.title: Create only after reviewing the rule
UserGuide.firewall.dialogActions.text: Check direction, protocol, and port before submitting. The guide demonstrates the form and never submits it.
UserGuide.firewall.map.title: Return to the topology to verify the result
UserGuide.firewall.map.text: Each line is an allowed connection and its label shows the port. Select a machine to inspect its own rules.
UserGuide.domain.configForm.title: Connection Settings opens the complete form
UserGuide.domain.configForm.text: Enter the Cloudflare Account ID and an API token with minimum required permissions. The default DNS target supports reverse proxy publishing. The guide never saves credentials.
UserGuide.domain.recordForm.title: Adding a DNS record opens the full form
UserGuide.domain.recordForm.text: Choose A, AAAA, CNAME, or another type, then set name, content, TTL, and proxy behavior. The guide never creates the record.
UserGuide.emptySimulation.title: Run through the complete flow in a simulation
UserGuide.emptySimulation.text: This page currently has no data, so the guide uses an example tailored to the page to demonstrate opening details, switching settings, and using the primary action. Nothing is saved.
UserGuide.adminHome.title: Admin Home
UserGuide.adminHome.intro.title: See what needs your attention first
UserGuide.adminHome.intro.text: This is the administrator's workbench: operating numbers at the top, the AI Operations Assistant in the middle, and below it your to-dos sorted by urgency into "Handle now" and "Sometime today".
UserGuide.adminHome.freshness.title: When the data was updated and how complete it is
UserGuide.adminHome.freshness.text: The home page refreshes itself every 30 seconds and pauses while the tab is hidden. An orange notice such as "Some connections unavailable" or "Latest data unavailable" means the numbers below may be incomplete; hover over it to read the full reason.
UserGuide.adminHome.stats.title: Nodes and machines at a glance
UserGuide.adminHome.stats.text: "Nodes" shows online / total, while VM and LXC show running / total, across every PVE connection. These are for information only; clicking a card takes you to platform monitoring or resource management.
UserGuide.adminHome.assistant.title: Ask the AI Operations Assistant
UserGuide.adminHome.assistant.text: Type a question or a VM you want checked; nothing is sent until you click "Start Asking". The suggested questions below only fill in the input box. Once the conversation starts, "Expand Chat" lets it fill the page and "Ask Another Question" clears it so you can start over.
UserGuide.adminHome.urgent.title: Handle now: things already going wrong
UserGuide.adminHome.urgent.text: Lists nodes and VMs whose CPU, RAM or disk is over the threshold, offline nodes, suspected mining incidents awaiting action, and background tasks that failed or were blocked in the last 7 days. A problem reported both live and as an alert appears only once; click a row to go to that machine or the related page.
UserGuide.adminHome.today.title: Sometime today: reviews waiting on you
UserGuide.adminHome.today.text: Machine requests (including spec changes), class batch provisioning and AI API requests each get one row, and the number is how many are waiting for review. Click a row to open that review list. When nothing is pending, it reads "No requests awaiting review".
UserGuide.teacherHome.title: Teacher Home
UserGuide.teacherHome.intro.title: Keep track of your classes and schedule
UserGuide.teacherHome.intro.text: Teacher Home brings together the status of your classes and your upcoming sessions. Every card and row is clickable and jumps straight to the matching detail page.
UserGuide.teacherHome.createClass.title: Start a new class here
UserGuide.teacherHome.createClass.text: "Create Class" opens the class setup flow, where you choose the students, the class schedule and the machines each student gets. After you submit, an administrator has to approve it before the machines are batch-provisioned.
UserGuide.teacherHome.metrics.title: What the two summary cards mean
UserGuide.teacherHome.metrics.text: The preparing count under "Active Classes" covers classes being set up, waiting for review, being provisioned or partially failed; "Next Class" is the date of the nearest session.
UserGuide.teacherHome.classes.title: Upcoming classes and machine status
UserGuide.teacherHome.classes.text: Sorted by the next session time, up to 4 classes. Active classes show what share of machines is ready, and classes still in planning show "Continue setup". To see every class, click "All Classes".
UserGuide.quickCreate.title: Quick Practice
UserGuide.quickCreate.intro.title: Launch a whole environment, no review
UserGuide.quickCreate.intro.text: This page lists published environments that are open for quick practice. Pick one and its machines are created right away, with no request or review needed. If the page is empty, no environment is open for quick practice yet.
UserGuide.quickCreate.grid.title: Each folder is one environment
UserGuide.quickCreate.grid.text: A folder is a complete practice environment and may hold several machines that connect to each other. The front cover shows the environment's name and description.
UserGuide.quickCreate.sheets.title: The sheets inside are the machines
UserGuide.quickCreate.sheets.text: Each sheet stands for one machine that will be created, labeled with its name and role; a monitor icon means a VM and a terminal icon means an LXC. When there are many machines, the last sheet shows how many more there are.
UserGuide.quickCreate.meta.title: Total resources and time allowed
UserGuide.quickCreate.meta.text: Under the cover you'll find the combined CPU and memory for the whole set, plus how many hours you can use it. These resources count against your usage quota, so you can't launch if you don't have enough left.
UserGuide.quickCreate.open.title: Click a folder to review first
UserGuide.quickCreate.open.text: Clicking only opens the launch confirmation page, where you can check each machine's specs and the usage rules. No machines are created at this point.
UserGuide.quickPractice.title: Launch Quick Practice
UserGuide.quickPractice.intro.title: Review the environment before launching
UserGuide.quickPractice.intro.text: This page lists the machines this environment will create and the rules for using them. Launch only once everything looks right. If you change your mind, click "Back" at the top right and nothing is created.
UserGuide.quickPractice.summary.title: Name, machine count and hours
UserGuide.quickPractice.summary.text: The top shows the environment's name and description; the tags are, in order, the number of machines, the hours you can use it and the environment version. The whole set is approved automatically, but CPU, memory, disk and the number of machines can't be changed.
UserGuide.quickPractice.machines.title: Machines to be created
UserGuide.quickPractice.machines.text: Lists each machine's name, role, whether it's a VM or LXC, and its CPU, memory and disk. The "Environment Total" at the bottom is exactly how much of your quota this launch will use.
UserGuide.quickPractice.rules.title: The whole set is reclaimed when time runs out
UserGuide.quickPractice.rules.text: When the hours are up, the system automatically deletes every machine in the set and nothing on them is kept, so back up anything important yourself. You can only have one quick practice set at a time, and launch at most 3 within 24 hours.
UserGuide.quickPractice.launch.title: Launching starts building right away
UserGuide.quickPractice.launch.text: "Launch N Machines" submits immediately and builds the whole set, then takes you to "My Resources" to follow the progress. If you're over quota, the environment is full or you've hit the launch limit, you'll see a message and no machines are created.
UserGuide.account.title: Account Settings
UserGuide.account.tabs.title: Three tabs for managing your account
UserGuide.account.tabs.text: "Profile" holds your name, email, password, two-factor authentication and account deletion; "Appearance" adjusts colors and interface style; "About" has version and license information.
UserGuide.account.profile.title: Name, email and avatar
UserGuide.account.profile.text: Click "Edit" to change your name, email and avatar URL. You can also drop an image into the upload box next to your avatar, and it takes effect immediately. Changing your email sends a verification message to the new address, and your old email stays in use until you click the link. For accounts created through a sign-in service such as LDAP or Google, the email is managed by that service and can't be changed here.
UserGuide.account.password.title: Change your SkyLab password
UserGuide.account.password.text: This changes the password you use to sign in to SkyLab, not the login password of your machines. The new password must meet the complexity rules listed below it. After the update, every signed-in device (including this one) is signed out and you'll need to sign in again with the new password.
UserGuide.account.twoFactor.title: Add protection with an authenticator app
UserGuide.account.twoFactor.text: Click "Link authenticator app" and scan the QR code with your phone; from then on, signing in also asks for a 6-digit code. Disabling it requires a code too. If an administrator requires it for your account, you can't disable it yourself; if you lose your phone, ask an administrator to reset it.
UserGuide.account.delete.title: Permanently delete your account
UserGuide.account.delete.text: Deleting your account removes it and its related data for good, and you must type "DELETE" to confirm. If you still hold any provisioned machines, the deletion is refused until you clear them; administrator accounts can't delete themselves.
UserGuide.account.appearance.title: Adjust colors and interface style
UserGuide.account.appearance.text: Under "Colors" you can pick the primary color, background color and background pattern, or upload your own background image; "Interface" switches the style and color mode. These settings are saved only in this browser, so you'll need to set them again on another computer or browser.
UserGuide.account.presets.title: Apply a color theme in one click
UserGuide.account.presets.text: Clicking a theme applies its primary color, background color and background pattern together, and the appearance form above updates to match. To go back to the defaults, click "Reset to Defaults" at the right of the tab bar; any uploaded background image is deleted as well.
UserGuide.account.about.title: Version and open-source licenses
UserGuide.account.about.text: The left side shows the current version, commit and build time, with links to the AGPL-3.0 license, the source code and third-party notices. The right side lists the open-source packages this web interface uses directly. Include the version number from here when you report a problem.
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.title: Resource Management
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.intro.title: Every machine on the platform
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.intro.text: This page lists every user's VMs and LXC containers, including personal, shared, class and quick practice machines. The list refreshes automatically, and administrators can power machines on and off, open consoles or delete machines right here.
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.create.title: Create machines via the request form
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.create.text: "Create Resource" takes you to the request form on "My Requests", where you fill in specs and a usage window the same way regular users do. This page does not create machines by itself.
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.filters.title: Filter by status and search
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.filters.text: Use "All", "Running" and "Stopped" to show only machines in that state; the badge numbers count all machines and ignore the search. The search box next to them matches name, VMID, IP or owner, and every space-separated word must match.
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.table.title: Key details for each machine
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.table.text: "Source" shows whether a machine is personal, shared, class or quick practice, along with its owner. The small text under "Expiry Date" is the actual cutoff in your local time, and "∞ No expiry" means no expiry date is set. Links under the IP are public URLs published through the reverse proxy.
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.envGroup.title: Teaching environments shown as groups
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.envGroup.text: Machines in a course teaching environment or quick practice environment are grouped together; click the row to expand or collapse it. Machines in a group cannot be deleted one by one, and the menu on the far right offers "Start all" and "Shut down all".
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.row.title: Click a row to open its details
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.row.text: Click anywhere on a machine row (other than buttons and checkboxes) to open its detail page with monitoring, specs, snapshots and advanced settings. Once you have machines checked, clicking a row checks it instead of opening the page.
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.select.title: Check machines for batch actions
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.select.text: After you check machines, the toolbar turns into a batch bar where you can "Start" or "Shutdown" them all at once; "More" holds Reboot, Force Stop and Force Reset, and Delete sits on the far right. Each action is only sent to the machines it applies to (for example, Shutdown only goes to running ones). Shift-click to select a range.
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.actions.title: Console and power menu
UserGuide.resourceMgmt.actions.text: While a machine is running, click "Console" (VM) or "Terminal" (LXC) to connect to it; the button stays disabled while it boots. The ⋮ menu on the right has power actions such as start, shutdown and reboot, plus "Convert to template" (not for class machines) and "Delete", which removes the machine from PVE and cannot be undone.
UserGuide.requestReview.title: Request Review
UserGuide.requestReview.intro.title: Review machine and spec change requests
UserGuide.requestReview.intro.text: This page gathers the two kinds of requests users submit: "Creation Request" and "Spec Change". AI API key requests are handled separately in "AI API review", and machine deletions are carried out automatically by background jobs, so neither appears here.
UserGuide.requestReview.tabs.title: Switch lists by review status
UserGuide.requestReview.tabs.text: The page opens on "Pending", your work queue, which is listed in full without truncation. The other tabs show up to the latest 100 creation requests and 100 spec changes. The number on each tab is the request count for that status, and spec changes never become "Expired".
UserGuide.requestReview.list.title: Request list and search
UserGuide.requestReview.list.text: Requests are sorted newest first, and the icon tells a VM, LXC or spec change apart. Approved spec changes also show their apply progress in gray text, such as "Awaiting apply". Use the search box above to filter by host name, applicant or status.
UserGuide.requestReview.batch.title: Check pending requests to reject them in bulk
UserGuide.requestReview.batch.text: Only pending requests can be checked. Once you check some, the toolbar becomes a batch bar that offers only "Reject", with one review note shared by all of them. Approvals have to be done one at a time, because each one needs its resource assessment checked first.
UserGuide.requestReview.detail.title: Click a request to see its details
UserGuide.requestReview.detail.text: After you click a request on the left, this panel shows its type, specs, usage window, operating system, GPU, projected node and the reason given. It only shows the request you explicitly clicked, and it never switches to another one when the list refreshes.
UserGuide.requestReview.decision.title: Add a note, then approve or reject
UserGuide.requestReview.decision.text: Use "Review Notes" for the reason you approve or send back a request. For creation requests, "Approve" is only enabled once the resource assessment has finished and the time window has enough capacity. An approved spec change only takes effect after the requester clicks Apply, and if the machine has been deleted the request can only be rejected.
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.title: GPU Management
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.intro.title: GPU mappings on PVE
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.intro.text: This page lists the PCI resource mappings configured on each PVE connection and which VMs are currently using each GPU group. Mappings themselves are created in PVE's datacenter settings; this page cannot add new ones.
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.search.title: Search mappings or PCI addresses
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.search.text: Search by mapping name, description, node name or PCI address. For example, type a node name to see only the GPUs on that host.
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.table.title: Mapping type and specs
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.table.text: The name in the "Mapping" column is what users pick when they request a GPU, and the small text below it shows SR-IOV or Passthrough. With vGPU it also shows the mdev profile and the VRAM assigned to each instance.
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.pci.title: Nodes and PCI addresses
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.pci.text: Lists the nodes and PCI addresses in this mapping. When there are more than 3 addresses, consecutive ones are compressed into ranges; click the "N VF(s)" or "N device(s)" chip to expand the full list.
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.capacity.title: Availability and VRAM
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.capacity.text: "Available / Total" is how many instances can still be assigned out of the total capacity. For SR-IOV, the total is the number of instances that can actually be created, which may be lower than the VF count; in that case the VF count is shown below. When VRAM data is available, its usage is shown too, or "usage unknown" if it cannot be read.
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.usage.title: VMs in use and status
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.usage.text: Lists the VMs attached to this GPU group; a green dot means the VM is running, and hovering shows its VMID. The "Status" column next to it shows "Available", "x/y in use" or "Full", and "Unknown" when the total is 0.
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.delete.title: Think twice before removing a mapping
UserGuide.gpuMgmt.delete.text: The trash button deletes this mapping on PVE directly without checking whether any VM is using it, so VMs still configured with this GPU will fail to start afterwards. If several PVE connections have a mapping with the same name, the deletion is refused.
UserGuide.batchReview.title: Class Review
UserGuide.batchReview.intro.title: Review class batch provisioning
UserGuide.batchReview.intro.text: Requests that teachers submit to create machines for a class in bulk wait here for review. Machine nodes from the same class with the same status are merged into one row, so approving or rejecting handles the whole class at once.
UserGuide.batchReview.tabs.title: Switch lists by review result
UserGuide.batchReview.tabs.text: "Pending" holds the requests you need to handle. "Approved" includes not only newly approved batches but also those waiting, provisioning, completed or failed; cancelled batches only appear under "All".
UserGuide.batchReview.search.title: Search batches or courses
UserGuide.batchReview.search.text: Search by batch name, applicant, course name, resource type or status.
UserGuide.batchReview.list.title: Batch request list
UserGuide.batchReview.list.text: A graduation-cap icon marks a class batch and a server icon marks a single batch. Each row shows the number of VMs and the applicant, sorted by submission time with the newest first.
UserGuide.batchReview.detail.title: Click a batch to see what's inside
UserGuide.batchReview.detail.text: After you click a batch on the left, this panel lists the course, resource type, VM count, specs and template, along with "Provisioning Progress" and the batch members. For batches with a recurring schedule, click "View upcoming windows" to preview the next power-on windows.
UserGuide.batchReview.decision.title: Approval starts provisioning right away
UserGuide.batchReview.decision.text: Fill in "Review Notes" and click "Approve" or "Reject"; a confirmation dialog follows. Once approved, the system immediately starts creating the machines in the background, and you can follow the progress in the "Approved" tab. Rejecting creates no machines.
UserGuide.templates.title: Templates
UserGuide.templates.intro.title: Turn a prepared environment into a template
UserGuide.templates.intro.text: A template is a read-only master image made from a machine that already has its software and settings in place, so you can quickly clone machines with the same environment from it. This list shows the templates you created plus the ones others have set to "Visible to Everyone".
UserGuide.templates.create.title: Create a template from a VM
UserGuide.templates.create.text: Click "Create from VM", pick a machine whose environment is ready, and give it a name. Note: conversion shuts the source machine down; afterwards it is removed from your resources and becomes the template's source machine, so it can no longer be used as a regular machine. This cannot be undone.
UserGuide.templates.table.title: What the template columns mean
UserGuide.templates.table.text: VMID is the template's ID on PVE, and Type is either qemu (VM) or lxc (container). With visibility "Private" only you can use it; once set to "Visible to Everyone", other teachers can clone it and students can pick it in the request form. The version goes up by one each time an update cycle is finished.
UserGuide.templates.badges.title: Warning labels next to the name
UserGuide.templates.badges.text: "Password not settable by the platform" means no cloud-init was detected during conversion, so cloned machines keep the template's original username and password; it clears automatically after you install cloud-init in the template and finish an update cycle. "Missing on PVE" means PVE can no longer find this template — it may have been deleted by hand.
UserGuide.templates.status.title: What each template status means
UserGuide.templates.status.text: "Creating" means the machine is being shut down and converted; the page refreshes on its own. Only "Ready" templates can be cloned. "Update cycle in progress" means a new version is being edited. When it shows "Failed", the reason appears under the name and you can use "Retry Conversion" from the menu.
UserGuide.templates.menu.title: Actions in the "⋯" menu
UserGuide.templates.menu.text: "Clone" creates machines straight from the template (Ready templates only). "Edit / Visibility" changes the name, description, visibility, GPU requirement, default specs, and attachments; a "Manual" item appears when there are attachments. "Delete Template" also deletes the template disk on PVE, and is refused while machines cloned from it still exist.
UserGuide.templates.cycle.title: Edit a template with an update cycle
UserGuide.templates.cycle.text: The template itself is read-only, so to change its contents choose "Start Update Cycle" from the menu: the system copies a temporary master machine into your resource list. When you are done editing, come back and choose "Finish Update (promote to new version)" to turn it into the new version and retire the old one. If you change your mind, "Cancel Update Cycle" reclaims the temporary machine.
UserGuide.aiApiReview.title: Request Review
UserGuide.aiApiReview.intro.title: Review AI API key requests
UserGuide.aiApiReview.intro.text: Key requests that users submit on the AI API page all land here. Once you approve one, the system immediately issues the applicant a key starting with ccai_, which they can see on their own AI API page.
UserGuide.aiApiReview.tabs.title: Switch by review status
UserGuide.aiApiReview.tabs.text: "Pending" is shown by default, and the numbers are the count for each status. Use "Approved" and "Rejected" to look back at history, or "All" to list every status. Each tab shows at most the latest 100 requests, and the page refreshes automatically.
UserGuide.aiApiReview.table.title: Request list
UserGuide.aiApiReview.table.text: Each row is one request: applicant, key name, purpose, status, and when it was submitted and reviewed. For requests not reviewed yet, the review time shows "Not yet reviewed".
UserGuide.aiApiReview.purpose.title: Read the purpose carefully first
UserGuide.aiApiReview.purpose.text: Purposes longer than 60 characters are cut off; hover over one to read it in full. The confirmation dialog opened by "Approve" or "Reject" also shows the complete purpose.
UserGuide.aiApiReview.actions.title: Approve or reject a request
UserGuide.aiApiReview.actions.text: Both "Approve" and "Reject" open a confirmation dialog first, where you can add review notes before submitting. An approved key's validity starts counting from the moment of approval (using the duration chosen in the request), and approval fails if the platform's public AI API URL has not been set yet. A review cannot be changed afterwards; this column then shows the review notes instead.
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.title: Key Management
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.intro.title: All AI API keys at a glance
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.intro.text: This page lists every user's AI API keys, showing the holder, requested purpose, last use, and status. Keys can only be issued through request review, so you cannot add one here.
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.status.title: Switch by key status
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.status.text: Only "Active" keys are shown by default. "Disabled" covers expired, revoked, and deleted keys, which the Status column labels as "Disabled" or "Deleted"; "All" ignores status. The numbers on each tab follow your current search and filters.
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.filter.title: Filter by role and creation time
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.filter.text: Click "Filter" to narrow the list by user role (Student / Teacher / Administrator) and creation time (last 7 or 30 days). Choices apply immediately, and the button shows how many conditions are in effect.
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.search.title: Find a specific key
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.search.text: Search by key name, user name, email, or key prefix. If someone reports a leaked key, the prefix tells you exactly which one it is.
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.table.title: Key list
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.table.text: Each row shows the key name with the holder's email, the owner's name, the requested purpose, activity, status, and creation date, newest first. Paging buttons appear below once there are more than 50 keys.
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.activity.title: Check usage in the Activity column
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.activity.text: "Activity" is the time of the key's most recent call; keys that were never called show "Never used". Consider deleting keys that have sat unused for a long time.
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.revoke.title: Delete an active key
UserGuide.aiApiKeys.revoke.text: "Delete" only appears on active keys. After you confirm, new calls fail immediately and the user can no longer see the key — this cannot be undone. Calls already in progress still finish, and usage records are kept.
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.title: AI Usage Monitoring
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.intro.title: Track site-wide AI usage and health
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.intro.text: This page brings together calls users make with their keys through the AI API, usage of the platform's built-in AI features (template recommendations, AI navigation, Teacher Judge, and more), and the runtime status of the AI Gateway and each model.
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.actions.title: Time range and Grafana
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.actions.text: "Last 7 days / Last 30 days / Last 90 days" changes the summary, trend chart, and details below all at once. When the monitoring stack is enabled, a "View details in Grafana" button also appears.
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.metrics.title: The three summary metrics
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.metrics.text: The figures under Call Count and Error rate compare against the previous period of the same length: call count as a percentage, error rate in percentage points (pp), with a rising error rate shown in red. Total Tokens covers only the currently selected period.
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.trend.title: Call and error trend
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.trend.text: Use the switch at the top right to show calls, tokens, failed calls, error rate, or average latency, and hover over the chart for the full numbers of that slot. The last 7 days are plotted by hour; longer periods are plotted by day.
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.health.title: Issues that need attention
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.health.text: "System status" only appears when something is wrong — for example usage data failed to load, the AI Gateway is not ready, models are offline or degraded, or the error rate reaches 5% or rises noticeably over the previous period. Click any item to jump straight to the matching details below.
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.models.title: Model runtime status
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.models.text: Lists each model's runtime status (Online / Degraded / Offline), healthy and unhealthy deployment counts, and its calls, tokens, failure rate, and average latency in the period. Model names that have calls are clickable and take you to that model's API key calls.
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.proxy.title: API key call details
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.proxy.text: Every call users make with their own keys, filterable by "All / Success / Failed". "First token" is how long it took to receive the first token. When "Token evidence" says "Missing upstream", the model did not report usage, so tokens are recorded as 0 and no output rate is computed. Only the latest 100 calls in the period are loaded, and search only looks within them.
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.template.title: Built-in AI and per-user usage
UserGuide.aiMonitoring.template.text: "Template Calls" are the call records of the platform's built-in AI features (template recommendations, AI navigation, Teacher Judge). The "User Usage" tab next to it adds both sources together, making it easy to spot the heaviest users.
UserGuide.courseCms.title: Course Management
UserGuide.courseCms.intro.title: Build the online course for a class
UserGuide.courseCms.intro.text: Write the learning content students see on their course page here. It is organized as "Learning path › Room › Task", with questions attached to each task; the other tab shows students' progress in real time.
UserGuide.courseCms.tree.title: The course content tree on the left
UserGuide.courseCms.tree.text: Click a name to select it and the arrow to expand or collapse it. An expanded path ends with "Add room" and an expanded room with "Add task"; type a title and press Enter to create and select it, or Esc to cancel.
UserGuide.courseCms.addPath.title: Add a learning path
UserGuide.courseCms.addPath.text: Click "+" to open "Add learning path", then choose a "Linked class" and enter the path name. A class can link to only one path, so classes that already have one are not listed.
UserGuide.courseCms.workspace.title: The right side edits only the selected level
UserGuide.courseCms.workspace.text: Names, difficulty and teaching content (Markdown) are sent only when you click "Save"; switching nodes or tabs with unsaved changes asks you to confirm first. "Publish"/"Unpublish", "Linked class" and questions take effect as soon as you click them. Students cannot see a path while it is still a draft.
UserGuide.courseCms.progressTab.title: Switch to student progress
UserGuide.courseCms.progressTab.text: The "Student progress" tab shows how far each student has got. If the content editor has unsaved changes, you will be asked to confirm before the tab switches.
UserGuide.courseCms.progressToolbar.text: Pick a path from the drop-down. While the badge next to it says "Live updating", the report refreshes as soon as a student answers; when it says "Connection lost", the numbers may be out of date and the page reconnects automatically.
UserGuide.courseCms.progressTable.title: Each student's completion
UserGuide.courseCms.progressTable.text: "Overall progress" is the completion percentage for the whole path, and each following column shows one room's completed questions out of the total. Until someone answers, you will see "No submissions yet".
UserGuide.courseTemplates.title: Teaching Environments
UserGuide.courseTemplates.intro.title: Define the machines each student gets
UserGuide.courseTemplates.intro.text: A teaching environment is a set of 1 to 3 machines plus the connection rules between them. Publishing locks the version, and both class provisioning and quick practice use it to give every student their own copy.
UserGuide.courseTemplates.create.title: Create a new teaching environment
UserGuide.courseTemplates.create.text: Click "Create teaching environment" to open the editor. Drafts save automatically, so you don't have to finish in one go; an environment can only be used by classes or quick practice after it is published.
UserGuide.courseTemplates.controls.title: Filter by status or search
UserGuide.courseTemplates.controls.text: The numbers next to "All", "Published" and "Draft" are the count for each status; the search box matches environment names and descriptions.
UserGuide.courseTemplates.table.title: Each row is one environment
UserGuide.courseTemplates.table.text: Each row shows how many machines a student gets, the total CPU and RAM, the version, how it is offered (formal course, quick practice or both), how many classes use it, and its status. Click a row to open it in the editor.
UserGuide.courseTemplates.rowActions.tex: The trash can only deletes environments that have never been used by a class or practice session, and it cannot be undone; the arrow opens the environment, just like clicking the row. A published environment only lets you change its name, purpose and usage — to change the machines, create a separate environment.
UserGuide.courseTemplateEditor.title: Teaching Environment Editor
UserGuide.courseTemplateEditor.intro.tex: The editor has two steps: "Basic Info" and "Machine Configuration". Every change to a draft is saved automatically, and a "Retry" button appears at the top if syncing fails; click "Back" to return to the environment list.
UserGuide.courseTemplateEditor.name.text: This is the name teachers see when they choose an environment for a class. A draft can leave it blank for now, but it must be filled in before publishing, or publishing is blocked and the field is highlighted in red.
UserGuide.courseTemplateEditor.usage.tex: "Usage" decides whether the published environment is offered to formal courses, quick practice, or both. It can still be changed after publishing.
UserGuide.courseTemplateEditor.files.tex: You can choose several files at once. Uploads and deletions take effect immediately and are not tied to draft saving. A brand-new environment accepts uploads only after its first autosave has created it.
UserGuide.courseTemplateEditor.saveBasic: A published environment is not saved automatically: after changing its name, purpose or usage, click "Save basics" to send the changes. Its machine configuration is frozen and can no longer be edited.
UserGuide.courseTemplateEditor.addBar.te: Under "Source", pick an existing template or add a new VM/LXC spec from a base image, then click "Add machine" — up to 3 machines per student. "Add connection" only sets up machine-to-machine access or published services; internet access is fully open by default.
Drag a line from one machine to another to let them talk, or to the internet to publish a service; click a line to see its details or delete it. Click a machine to edit its name, role and CPU/RAM/Disk on the right — disk can only grow. A published version is view-only.
UserGuide.courseTemplateEditor.publish.t: "Publish" first checks the name, the number of machines and the connection settings. Once published, the version is locked for good and becomes available to classes or quick practice; if you came here from class setup, you are taken back to the class afterwards.
UserGuide.classManagement.title: Class Management
UserGuide.classManagement.intro.title: Manage the classes you teach
UserGuide.classManagement.intro.text: Each ticket is one class, moving from planning through pending review and provisioning to ready for class. Opening a class that is still in planning takes you back to the setup flow; any other class opens its class page, where you manage students, machines and weekly content.
UserGuide.classManagement.create.title: Create a new class
UserGuide.classManagement.create.text: "Create class" opens a five-step setup flow: class & schedule, student list, teaching environment, weekly tasks and confirmation. Saved steps are kept as a draft, so you can click the ticket later to pick up where you left off.
UserGuide.classManagement.filters.title: Filter by class status
UserGuide.classManagement.filters.text: "Building" combines pending review and provisioning; "Needs attention" appears only when some machines in a class failed to build. Use the search box on the right to find a class by name.
UserGuide.classManagement.archived.title: Ended classes are hidden by default
UserGuide.classManagement.archived.text: Check "Show ended" to list archived classes; the number in brackets is how many there are.
UserGuide.classManagement.ticket.title: What a ticket shows
UserGuide.classManagement.ticket.text: The front shows the weekly class time, how many minutes early machines boot, and the term dates. The barcode on the right is progress: for a class in planning it counts finished setup items (students, environment, tasks); otherwise it counts machines already built.
UserGuide.classManagement.batch.title: Archive and reclaim in bulk
UserGuide.classManagement.batch.text: Tick the box in a ticket's top-right corner and the toolbar turns into a batch bar with "Archive and reclaim". This stops upcoming schedules and reclaims every machine in those classes; it cannot be undone, but class and course records are kept.
UserGuide.classSetup.title: Create Class
UserGuide.classSetup.intro.title: Set up a class step by step
UserGuide.classSetup.intro.text: Complete the five steps in order and submit for provisioning; once an administrator approves, a machine set is built for every student. Each step is saved only when you click "Save and continue", and this tour covers just the step you are on.
UserGuide.classSetup.stepper.title: The step bar
UserGuide.classSetup.stepper.text: A check mark means that step is saved on the server. Class, students and teaching environment are required, and later steps stay locked until they are saved; weekly tasks are optional.
UserGuide.classSetup.basic.title: Class and fixed schedule
UserGuide.classSetup.basic.text: The class name is required, and the class location appears on students' daily schedule. The start and end dates plus the weekly class time generate every week's session automatically.
UserGuide.classSetup.advanced.title: Power times are in advanced settings
UserGuide.classSetup.advanced.text: Expand it to set the term, "Boot lead time" and "Shutdown after class": machines start ahead of class and shut down automatically afterwards as configured. Leave them alone to keep the defaults.
UserGuide.classSetup.emails.title: Paste student emails
UserGuide.classSetup.emails.text: Separate them with new lines, commas or semicolons. Accounts that don't exist or aren't students are not added; they stay in the box, highlighted in red, so you can fix or remove them before continuing.
UserGuide.classSetup.csv.title: Or import a CSV
UserGuide.classSetup.csv.text: The file is imported as soon as you choose it — no need to save. Accounts that can't be added are merged back into the box for you to deal with.
UserGuide.classSetup.groupImport.title: Or import from a group
UserGuide.classSetup.groupImport.text: Import a group an administrator has set up (such as one school class) in one go. Only the group's students are brought in, and it copies the list as it is now — later changes to the group won't affect this class.
UserGuide.classSetup.roster.title: Current class students
UserGuide.classSetup.roster.text: These students are already saved to the class, and you need at least one to continue. Duplicate accounts are skipped automatically, and the icon next to a student removes them.
UserGuide.classSetup.envList.title: Choose a teaching environment
UserGuide.classSetup.envList.text: Only published versions are listed, and each card shows the machines per student and total specs. After you submit for provisioning, everyone in the class gets the same set of machines.
UserGuide.classSetup.templatePause.title: When no environment fits
UserGuide.classSetup.templatePause.text: Click "Create a new class template" to build one first; the first two steps are already saved as a draft, and once the template is published you return to this step with it selected. "Continue later" takes you back to class management.
UserGuide.classSetup.publishWeeks.title: Publish filled-in weeks right away
UserGuide.classSetup.publishWeeks.text: When checked, every week with a topic becomes visible to students immediately; otherwise those weeks stay as drafts and must be published one by one later from the class's "Weekly Content".
UserGuide.classSetup.weeks.title: Weekly topics or checkpoints
UserGuide.classSetup.weeks.text: Weeks and dates come from the schedule, so you only need to fill in topics. This step is optional, and course files can be added in the class later.
UserGuide.classSetup.readiness.title: Capacity check
UserGuide.classSetup.readiness.text: The system checks whether there are enough resources for the number of students, the environment specs and the course period. When it passes, it lists the total machines, CPU, RAM, disk and IPs to reserve; when it fails, it explains why.
UserGuide.classSetup.summary.title: Review each step
UserGuide.classSetup.summary.text: The four rows match the earlier steps, and a check mark means the step is done; click any row to go back and change it.
UserGuide.classSetup.next.title: Save and continue
UserGuide.classSetup.next.text: A step is saved to the server only when you click "Save and continue". If you click "Previous" or jump with the step bar, unsaved changes are discarded after you confirm.
UserGuide.classSetup.provision.title: Submit for provisioning
UserGuide.classSetup.provision.text: "Finish setup and submit for provisioning" is enabled only after the capacity check passes. Submitting locks the students, environment and schedule and sends the class to an administrator for review; click "Submit later" if you're not ready yet.
UserGuide.classSetup.draft.title: Class draft summary
UserGuide.classSetup.draft.text: Always shows each step's progress and the estimated number of machines (students × machines per student); click a row to jump to any unlocked step.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.common.header.t: The header shows the term, location and class name, with the number of students, weeks and the weekly class time underneath. The tabs below the header go "Class Overview", "Add Students", "Teaching Environment" and "Weekly Content"; while the class is being set up, a check mark means that step is done.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.common.tabs.tit: Tabs once the class is active
UserGuide.classWorkspace.common.tabs.tex: After the class passes review and all machines are built, the steps become plain tabs and "Class Monitoring" and "AI Check" are added. Opening an active class from the class list takes you straight to "Class Monitoring".
UserGuide.classWorkspace.overview.title: Class Overview
UserGuide.classWorkspace.overview.action: "Back to class management" returns to the class list. The "⋯" menu has "Edit class & schedule" (only before you submit for provisioning), "Extend" for the end date, and "Archive and reclaim": archiving stops scheduling, cancels unfinished provisioning and reclaims every machine in the class, keeping only the class and course records.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.overview.status: This card tells you the next step for the class's current status. Once the student list and teaching environment are set, platform capacity is checked first, and only if it is sufficient can you click "Confirm and submit for provisioning". After submitting, the roster, environment and schedule are locked and sent to an administrator for review. If some machines fail to build, click "Retry failed items" here.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.overview.week.t: Shows the topic, date and file count for the current week (or the next class). "View all weeks" switches to "Weekly Content", where you edit each week's topic, files and publishing status.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.overview.machin: Before you submit for provisioning, this shows the estimated total from the number of students and machines per student; after provisioning it shows how many machines are ready. Click this row to switch to "Teaching Environment".
UserGuide.classWorkspace.overview.info.t: Expand "Class info" to see the course period, the "Boot lead time" before class, and the grace period for "Shutdown after class". To change them, use "Edit class & schedule" in the "⋯" menu at the top right.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.students.title: Add Students
UserGuide.classWorkspace.students.action: "Import CSV" reads the email or student ID in the first column (a bare student ID gets the school domain appended). "Import from group" brings in the students of a group an administrator has set up, such as one school class. "Add students" lets you paste several emails at once. Only registered student accounts are added; accounts that can't be found or aren't students are listed in the notice.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.students.list.t: Each row is one student: VMID is the ID of their class machine, and the "Machines" column shows how many are built. With a large class, use the search box above to find a name or email. Once you submit for provisioning the roster is locked and students can no longer be added or removed.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.students.remove: The button at the right of each row removes that student. When you tick several students, the search bar turns into a batch bar, and "Remove" removes all ticked students at once. You are always asked to confirm first.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.machines.title: Teaching Environment
UserGuide.classWorkspace.machines.choose: Published course environments are listed here. Clicking a card applies it to the class right away, and every student gets the same set of machines. An environment can't be applied if any machine in it isn't bound to an available template or image yet.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.machines.create: "Create new course environment" opens the course environment editor. Once you publish it you are brought back here with the new environment marked as suggested; click it to apply.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.machines.applie: After you submit for provisioning the environment is locked and can't be changed. This shows the machines per student, the number of students, and the CPU, memory and disk "Per student" and for the "Whole class" — the whole-class figure is what the course will consume.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.machines.public: Public services declared by the environment are listed here. Each student gets their own URL or external port, and once the class starts they can see their connection details on the course page.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.machines.topolo: This read-only canvas shows the connections between each student's machines and the services reachable from outside. Click a line to see its port details; "Internet Lines" at the top left shows each machine's outbound internet connection.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.weekly.title: Weekly Content
UserGuide.classWorkspace.weekly.list.tex: Every class session is laid out from the schedule. Each row sets the topic, the task files and whether students can see it. The top right shows how many weeks students can currently see.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.weekly.row.text: "Topic / task" is the title students see on the course page. Students see all class machines on each week's page.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.weekly.files.te: Drag files in or click to choose them; they are saved to the server as soon as the upload finishes. The × next to a file name deletes that file immediately.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.weekly.visibili: Students only see a week's topic and files on the course page when it is set to "Publish". If you click "Publish" before filling in a topic, you'll be asked to add one first.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.weekly.save.tex: Topics and publishing status are only stored when you click "Save weekly content"; leaving without saving loses your edits. After the class is archived this page is read-only.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.progress.title: Class Monitoring
UserGuide.classWorkspace.progress.locked: "Class Monitoring" opens only after the class passes review and every student's machines are built. Check "Class Overview" to see which step the class is on.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.progress.broadc: Pick one of your own running VMs from the dropdown to broadcast its screen to the whole class. The broadcast keeps going when you switch to other tabs; click "End broadcast" to stop it.
"Start all" and "Shut down all" act on every machine in the class (including the teacher's set) in batches, with progress shown alongside; shutting down asks for confirmation first. Machines started outside class time shut down automatically when the practice time is up.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.progress.toolba: When each student has several machines, choose which one to view on the left; on the right, switch between CPU and RAM usage. The figures below show machines powered on, average usage and the number of students under high load.
Each tile is one student (seat number and name). Darker means busier, light red is high load (≥ 80%), a dashed border means powered off and a dotted border means no data yet; it updates every 10 seconds. Click a running tile to open a VM's desktop (you can take control) or an LXC's terminal.
UserGuide.classWorkspace.progress.attent: Lists students under high load (highest first) and students whose machine is off during class; click a name to open that machine directly. If the whole class is off, it shows a single note instead of listing everyone.
UserGuide.aiJudge.title: AI Check
UserGuide.aiJudge.header.title: Let AI help check assignments
UserGuide.aiJudge.header.text: This page builds assignment checks for the class: list what to check, the system turns those items into check scripts and runs them on every student's machine, and finally you review the results and leave feedback.
UserGuide.aiJudge.tabs.title: Class tabs
UserGuide.aiJudge.tabs.text: This is the class's "AI Check" tab. If you switch tabs or go back to class management with an unsaved proposal, message or review, you are asked before leaving.
UserGuide.aiJudge.locked.title: Class not active yet
UserGuide.aiJudge.locked.text: AI Check is available only after the class passes review and every student's machines are built.
UserGuide.aiJudge.sessions.title: Weeks
UserGuide.aiJudge.sessions.text: Each week has one check, and students see it on that week's page. Click a week to set up its check; switch between "Task settings" and "Teacher review" at the top. For weeks with a check, "⋯" moves or copies it to another empty week, or deletes it.
UserGuide.aiJudge.empty.title: Create this week's check
UserGuide.aiJudge.empty.text: The selected week has no check yet. Click "Create this week's check", then ask AI Check to draft this week's items.
UserGuide.aiJudge.rubric.title: Task settings: items
UserGuide.aiJudge.rubric.text: Each row is a checkpoint and its check method. In "Auto-check support", "Supported" means a script can judge it, "Missing info" means more detail is needed, and "Teacher check" leaves it to your own judgment. Click the arrow at the start of a row to expand its check details.
UserGuide.aiJudge.assistant.title: AI Check
UserGuide.aiJudge.assistant.text: Describe what you want to check, or use "Attach file" to upload a rubric (.md, .txt, .doc, .docx, .pdf), and the assistant proposes check items. A proposal is only written into the checklist on the left after you click "Apply".
UserGuide.aiJudge.saveBuild.title: Build scripts
UserGuide.aiJudge.saveBuild.text: "Build scripts" first saves and reviews every item, and once they all pass it builds the check scripts automatically. While items are still incomplete the button looks dimmed; clicking it tells you what's missing.
UserGuide.aiJudge.review.title: Run and review
UserGuide.aiJudge.review.text: "Run all" runs every approved script on each student's matching machine; machines must be on, and students whose machines are off are marked as not run. Expand a student to mark each check "Passed" or "Failed", write a weekly reply below the check results, then click "Save" to save this student's decisions and reply together.
UserGuide.adminUsers.title: User Management
UserGuide.adminUsers.intro.title: Manage every account on the platform
UserGuide.adminUsers.intro.text: This page manages all platform accounts: create and edit users, assign the student, teacher or admin role, disable accounts, review self-registration requests, and require two-factor authentication per account.
UserGuide.adminUsers.add.title: Create an account manually
UserGuide.adminUsers.add.text: Click "Add User" to create an account directly with an email, password and role — no email verification or approval needed. The password must be at least 8 characters and include uppercase, lowercase, a number and a symbol.
UserGuide.adminUsers.groups.title: Organize accounts into groups
UserGuide.adminUsers.groups.text: "Groups" lets you create, rename and delete groups (such as one class) and import members from a CSV. Teachers can import a group's students straight into a class roster; only administrators can maintain groups.
UserGuide.adminUsers.registration.title: Self-registration and approval
UserGuide.adminUsers.registration.text: These three switches save as soon as you toggle them; there is no separate save button. "Allow self-registration" controls whether new accounts can sign up from the login page. "Allow account creation on first Google login" separately controls whether a Google address without an account gets one on its first login. With "Require administrator approval" on, new accounts can only be used after you approve them below. Turning registration off does not stop existing accounts from signing in.
UserGuide.adminUsers.pending.title: Handle pending registrations
UserGuide.adminUsers.pending.text: New accounts waiting for administrator approval are listed here. "Approve" lets them sign in; "Reject" leaves the account unusable. When nothing is pending, this area shows an empty notice.
UserGuide.adminUsers.summary.title: Account counts at a glance
UserGuide.adminUsers.summary.text: Total users, active accounts, teachers and admins are counted across all accounts and are not affected by the search below.
UserGuide.adminUsers.row.title: Each row is one account
UserGuide.adminUsers.row.text: Each row shows the role and status. An "LDAP" tag means the password is managed by the campus directory; "2FA" means two-factor authentication is set up. Tick the boxes on the left to enable, disable, add to a group, remove from a group or delete accounts in bulk — you cannot select or delete yourself. The search box above matches name, email or role, and once groups exist the menu next to it shows only one group's members.
UserGuide.adminUsers.security.title: Require two-factor authentication per account
UserGuide.adminUsers.security.text: Tick "Require two-factor authentication" in the edit dialog and save; the user must then set up an authenticator app at their next sign-in and cannot turn it off themselves. If they lose their phone, click "Reset two-factor authentication" in the same dialog to remove it, which also ends all of their current sessions. This step only opens the dialog as a demo and saves nothing.
UserGuide.pveConnections.title: PVE Management
UserGuide.pveConnections.intro.title: Manage the PVE hosts the platform uses
UserGuide.pveConnections.intro.text: The upper half lists PVE connections; each connection is its own entry point (a single host or a whole cluster). The lower half lists the nodes synced from all connections. When a machine is created, the platform picks one of these nodes to place it on.
UserGuide.pveConnections.add.title: Add a PVE connection
UserGuide.pveConnections.add.text: Click "Add Connection" and enter the host, API user and password. The first connection automatically becomes the default. Saving does not sync on its own — click "Sync" on that row so its nodes and storage show up.
UserGuide.pveConnections.resources.title: Per-cluster resource settings
UserGuide.pveConnections.resources.text: The pool, storage, gateway IP, local subnet and default node under "This Cluster's Resource Settings" apply only to machines created through this connection, so each cluster can use different values. Leaving Backup Storage blank means machine backups are not offered on this cluster. This step only opens the form as a demo and saves nothing.
UserGuide.pveConnections.row.title: Connection overview
UserGuide.pveConnections.row.text: Each row shows the connection name, address and API user. The "Default" tag marks the default connection; on the right are its enabled state and the number of synced nodes. Click the pencil icon to edit a connection — leave the password blank to keep it unchanged.
UserGuide.pveConnections.actions.title: Test, sync and delete
UserGuide.pveConnections.actions.text: "Test" only checks whether the saved settings can reach PVE and changes nothing. "Sync" fetches the nodes and storage again and refreshes the list below. A connection that still has machines cannot be deleted, and the default connection cannot be deleted while other connections exist. "Force Delete" is offered only when PVE is unreachable and the check cannot be made.
UserGuide.pveConnections.nodes.title: Node availability and priority
UserGuide.pveConnections.nodes.text: "Online" and "Offline" reflect the most recent sync. The switch on the right takes effect immediately: a disabled node no longer receives new machines, while existing machines are unaffected. Use edit to change a node's API address and priority; lower numbers win, and priority only breaks ties when nodes have similar placement scores.
UserGuide.scheduler.title: Resource Scheduling
UserGuide.scheduler.intro.title: Scheduling settings shared by all clusters
UserGuide.scheduler.intro.text: This page sets the placement, overcommit and scheduled-boot parameters shared by every PVE connection. Each cluster's own pool, storage and subnet are not here — edit the connection on the "PVE Management" page instead.
UserGuide.scheduler.placement.title: Overcommit ratios set how much can be allocated
UserGuide.scheduler.placement.text: A "CPU Overcommit Ratio" of 2 allows up to 2 vCPUs per physical core; a "Disk Overcommit Ratio" of 1 means disks are not overcommitted. The higher the "Node Reassignment Cost", the more the platform prefers to keep a machine on its current node. Cards marked "Takes effect immediately" apply to the very next placement after you save.
UserGuide.scheduler.thresholds.title: How busy nodes are penalized
UserGuide.scheduler.thresholds.text: These values decide how busy nodes lose points during placement: peak margins reserve room for CPU and RAM spikes, LoadAvg is always measured per physical core, and the resource weights set how much CPU, RAM and disk each matter. If unsure, keep the defaults.
UserGuide.scheduler.boot.title: Scheduled boots run in batches
UserGuide.scheduler.boot.text: Before a usage window starts, the platform powers machines on ahead of time according to "Boot Lead Time (minutes)", "Boot Batch Size" machines at a time with the set interval between batches, so storage is not overwhelmed by simultaneous boots. "Window Grace Period (minutes)" is how long to wait after the window ends before shutting down automatically. This card applies from the next scheduler cycle.
UserGuide.scheduler.practice.title: Practice sessions and expiry warnings
UserGuide.scheduler.practice.text: When a student starts a machine outside a usage window, it shuts down automatically after "Practice Session (hours)", with a reminder "Practice Warning (minutes)" before the end.
